newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian nurse's brother rejects mercy for accused.
newsitem.headline: Australian nurse's brother rejects mercy for accused.

text.p: The family of an Australian nurse murdered in Saudi Arabia ruled out a clemency appeal on Monday for two British nurses who could face public beheading if convicted of her murder.
"We think they should receive whatever the law dictates is the maximum penalty -- whatever it is," the nurse's brother, Frank Gilford, told Reuters.
"When you consider the way my sister died, I cannot see any reason to do other than what we have decided," he said.
Gilford's sister Yvonne, 55, was stabbed four times, battered with a hammer and smothered in her dormitory at the King Fahd military medical complex eastern Saudi Arabia on December 11.

British nurses Lucille McLauchlan, 31, and Deborah Parry, 41, have been charged with murder, but their lawyer has said they had signed confessions in the hope they would be sent home. The penalty for murder in Saudi Arabia under Islamic sharia law is beheading, but the sentence can be commuted at the request of the victim's family.
The family can also ask for financial settlement, called diah or blood money, instead of the death penalty.

Gilford, a 59-year-old courier driver from the small farming town of Jamestown, 200 kilometres north of Adelaide, said in a telephone interview that he believed the family's decision not to appeal for clemency had upset the British and Australian governments.
However, he said the decision came in response to the deliberate and vicious nature of his sister's death.
"It was the way she died; she was belted, they reckon she was hit with a teapot or kettle or something, then she was stabbed, and then she was smothered," he said.

"If she had just been hit with a kettle and fell down and died or she got smacked or just knifed once, well fair enough you say that might have been an accident or (an act of passion)... you would look at it differently," he said.
"There are so many brutal murders around which I think need the death penalty, even in Australia, for the real bad cases, the real dramatic cases," he said.
Gilford said he had faith in the police investigation and judicial processes in Saudi Arabia which would prove whether the two British nurses were guilty or innocent.
"If they prove them guilty, then they should take the full brunt of the law," he said.
He had had no contact from either the British nurses' defence or Saudi officials over the matter, he said.

Gilford said he and his elderly mother had last seen his sister, who had previously nursed in South Africa, England, and New Zealand, in May 1996 when she had left Australia to take up the 12 month contract in Saudi Arabia.
Her murder had come as "a terrific shock", he said, adding: "I do not think we have really come to terms with it even yet, it is going to take a while."
